papers.title: Gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Gratitude and savoring have great potential to support well-being in older age, but most studies on positive psychology interventions have been conducted among healthy young adults. This narrative review explored gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults, with or without dementia, including (a) the characteristics of these interventions, (b) their acceptability for older users, and (c) their effect on mental health. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: Scopus, PubMed, PsychInfo, Web of Science, and CINAHL were searched in December 2023 and April 2025. Studies were eligible if they examined gratitude or savoring interventions among older adults. Multi-component intervention studies were excluded. 2 researchers independently screened 2,423 studies and assessed methodological quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Numerical and narrative data were extracted and synthesized regarding intervention characteristics, acceptability, and effectiveness. RESULTS: Of the 11 included articles, 5 examined gratitude, 5 examined savoring, and 1 compared both. Only 1 study included participants with dementia. Adherence was generally high, suggesting a good fit, but participant evaluation was lacking. 4 acceptability themes were highlighted concerning the target group, setting and delivery mode, dosage, and content and tailoring. Most studies showed improved well-being and reduced psychopathology, although not consistently on all outcome measures. DISCUSSION AND IMPLICATIONS: There is initial evidence that gratitude and savoring interventions could be suitable to promote mental health among older adults with relatively preserved cognitive function. Future research should examine the need for tailoring in terms of dose, delivery method and content, and applicability to more diverse groups of older adults.

papers.title: Evaluating the effectiveness and cost-benefit of a worksite mental health program among manufacturing workers: A study protocol for a quasi-experimental study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mental health problems lead to the loss of about 12 billion workdays worldwide each year. This creates a major economic burden. In food manufacturing, workers often face various psychosocial stressors. These include high workload, time constraint, repetitive tasks, and low autonomy. These conditions can affect both mental health and work performance. Workplace mental health interventions have shown promising results in mental health improvement. However, most studies come from high-income countries and service sectors. There is still limited evidence from industrial settings in middle-income countries. To address this gap, a structured Worksite Mental Health Program (WMHP) was developed. METHOD: This study will employ a quasi-experimental two arm repeated measures design among workers from food manufacturing factories in Malaysia. The intervention group will receive an eight week WMHP including psychoeducation, mindfulness practices, progressive muscle relaxation, and breathing exercises. The comparison group will continue with routine workplace practices and receive a general mental health information pamphlet. Assessments will be carried out at baseline, one month post intervention, and at three months follow up. Primary outcomes include depression, anxiety, stress, and burnout. Secondary outcomes include job satisfaction, absenteeism, presenteeism, and economic outcomes. Changes over time will be analysed using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE). A cost-benefit analysis (CBA) will also be conducted to assess economic impact. ANTICIPATED RESULTS: The program is expected to improve mental health and work performance, while simultaneously reducing absenteeism and presenteeism. The economic evaluation is expected to demonstrate positive productivity gains associated with the program. CONCLUSION: This study will provide evidence on the effectiveness and economic value of a workplace mental health intervention in an industrial setting, informing workplace health strategies in Malaysia and similar contexts. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Thai Clinical Trials Registry (TCTR): TCTR20241217003.

papers.title: Mediators of age differences in well-being and psychological distress across adulthood.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Aging is associated with improvements in well-being and reductions in psychological distress. However, little is known about why this occurs. This study explored candidate psychological variables that may explain age differences in mental health. METHODS: We used cross-sectional data of 5712 Canadians aged 18-101 to explore associations between age and mental health, and then to investigate whether basic psychological needs (BPNs), loneliness, perceived control, mindfulness, optimism, and neuroticism mediated age's relationship with well-being and distress. RESULTS: Each variable in this study predicted age differences in mental health. We also found evidence that different mediators accounted for age differences in distress and well-being. For well-being, BPN fulfillment was the strongest mediator ( CONCLUSION: Our findings support the dual continuum of mental health with age and point to variables that may explain why older adults have greater well-being (e.g., because they have greater BPN fulfilment) and less distress (e.g., because they are less lonely). These variables are potential targets of intervention for those older adults whose mental health does not improve with age, as well as for younger adults whose mental health was poorer, on average.

papers.title: Predicting IGD treatment outcomes across interventions using a whole-brain functional connectome biomarker.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although treatment approaches have been explored in internet gaming disorder (IGD), however, little is known about the specific neural activity that is associated with treatment outcomes. This study aims to establish a treatment-sensitive network that reliably predicts treatment outcomes across different interventions for IGD. METHODS: Resting-state fMRI data were collected from 90 individuals with IGD who received one of three different intervention protocols (mindfulness meditation, approach bias modification, or retrieval-aversive conditioning training). Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) was used to build a treatment-sensitive network to predict individual symptom reduction, then validated them on the external dataset. These findings provide valuable empirical evidence for identifying biomarkers for IGD treatment and advance personalised therapeutic strategies. papers.title: Supporting incarcerated autistic individuals: evaluation of an autism awareness training for prison staff.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Prison environments are particularly challenging for autistic people experiencing incarceration due to a lack of knowledge and awareness of autism among prison staff. The study aimed to evaluate the level of satisfaction and perceived effectiveness of an autism awareness training for prison staff and to assess whether this training improves autism knowledge and reduces stigma towards autistic individuals in a prison setting. DESIGN/METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: The Autism Experience Circuit (AEC), an interactive autism awareness training, has been offered to prison staff. The training was evaluated through an online survey among 31 prison employees who participated in the AEC compared to a control group of 51 other staff members. FINDINGS: Results showed high satisfaction among AEC participants. They especially appreciated the interactive method. For most participants, the AEC led to increased knowledge and understanding of autism, as indicated by their assessment of goal achievement. A significant improvement in autism knowledge, but not in stigma towards autistic people, was found in the AEC group compared to the control group. ORIGINALITY/VALUE: These findings suggest that an autism awareness training can be a valuable first step in making prisons more accommodating for autistic individuals, but additional strategies are necessary to address stigma effectively.
